take: Brent’s push towards $120 on reports that four tankers struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz, alongside explosions at Iran’s Jask port, is the dominant crude story and it matters because a genuine Hormuz disruption would hit sour crude and product exports to Asia far harder than any headline risk premium suggests. The same Hormuz attack, now involving hull-mounted explosives on a tanker, is transmitting directly into freight as oil majors book billions in additional shipping liabilities from runaway tanker rates, whilst a coordinated dockworker mobilisation across 113 ports in 22 countries adds a separate layer of congestion risk. The inventory and positioning angle is thin on fresh data but telling: US refinery utilisation averaged above 95% between May and September, the highest for those months since 1998, so with ExxonMobil’s Gulf Coast refineries running at full capacity and diesel doing the heavy lifting on its doubled $15.4bn profit, the system has little slack to absorb a crude supply shock. The cross-market link to watch is the product crack versus freight: gasoline up 34% and heating oil up 74% into the midterms, with European refiners now seriously rethinking their phase-down programme, which normalises a tighter Atlantic Basin product balance just as tanker costs eat into delivered margins. Watch Hormuz transit reports and any confirmation of further mining or vessel strikes over the next 24 hours, plus whether Brent holds above $120 and whether the 113-port labour action escalates into sustained berth delays.
